title: 17 places in the Wilmington area that locals say are haunted
excerpt: These 17 spots in the Wilmington area are regarded as haunted by locals.
content:
Oct. 28, 2026, 5:00 a.m. ET

Wilmington is a place rich with history -- and that history has spawned countless stories of ghosts that still roam the Cape Fear region today. From phantom soldiers to a decapitated railroad worker, the area has it all when it comes to paranormal tales.

Some of the region's most recognizable historic sites and attractions come with eerie tales and many have even been the subject of paranormal investigations.

Whether you're looking to avoid these places or intentionally seek them out, here's a list of spots in the Wilmington area that some residents regard as haunted.

Battleship North Carolina

The Battleship North Carolina, which serves as a museum and historic site, is widely considered to be haunted, and was even featured on the show "Ghost Hunters." The ship participated in naval combat through World War II. In September 1942, the ship was struck by a torpedo during operations in the Pacific, killing five crew members. Some ghost stories claim those men still haunt the vessel.

Old Baldy Lighthouse

Local legends have also linked the lighthouse to the ghost of Theodosia Burr Alston, the daughter of former Vice President Aaron Burr. Theodosia Burr Alston disappeared at sea in 1813, and some claim she shipwrecked in Frying Pan Shoals -- or was captured by pirates nearby.

Bellamy Mansion

Visitors to this historic downtown mansion have reported seeing ghosts, including a woman dressed in gray. There are also stories of doors and windows unlocking and opening by themselves.

Fort Fisher State Historic Site

There were thousands of causalities when Union troops assaulted the Confederate fort toward the end of the Civil War, and some stories claim to have spotted dead soldiers lingering on the battlefield.

Charlie Brown’s Tavern

Located in Supply, this bar is among the newer spots to emerge as a potentially haunted location. Employees report ghostly figures, floating orbs of light and disembodied voices. The owners even recently called in a paranormal investigator to help get to the bottom of the disturbances.

St. James Cemetery

The story goes that Samuel Jocelyn was accidentally buried alive here in the early 1800s and later appeared as a ghost to his friend.

Maco

Once the crossroads of two railroads, Maco became legendary due to reports of a mysterious light that would appear in the area dating back to the 1880s. Traditionally, the story goes that the light was the ghost of railroad worker Joe Baldwin, who was beheaded in an accident, out looking for his head.

Lula’s

This pub located in downtown Wilmington is said to be haunted by a ghost named Cooter, a slave from the 1800s who was said to have been executed on the property.

The Brunswick Inn

A benevolent ghost named Tony allegedly haunts The Brunswick Inn. According to the tale, Antonio Caselatta, a harpist who played at the inn, drowned while out sailing near Bald Head Island. His spirit, however, returned to inn, and can sometimes even be hard playing the harp, the story goes.

Thalian Hall

This historic building in the heart of downtown is home to Wilmington’s theatrical community. It’s also apparently home to ghosts, including one story of "a tall, slender figure wearing a frock coat and knee-high boots in the Edwardian style" that came out of nowhere and disappeared just as quickly.

Bulluck Hospital

This small hospital on Front Street closed in the 1950s, but the old building remains. A story goes that a Wilmington police officer fell asleep in the adjacent alley and woke up to see a ghostly image of a little boy near his car.

Lattimer House

This historic home in downtown Wilmington was owned by Zebulon and Elizabeth Latimer. The Latimers had nine children, five of whom died before their 5th birthday. Some guests have reported seeing the faces of the children in the upstairs windows.

The Price-Gause House

Wilmington once held public executions near what is today the intersection of Fifth Avenue and Market Street, and some of those souls are said to have stuck around the area, particularly at the nearby Price-Gause House. The most famous, nicknamed George, is said to try to greet people from the porch in old-timey clothes. 

Oakdale Cemetery

Oakdale Cemetery is centuries old and, of course, contains thousands of graves. Unlike some entries on this list, no prominent ghostly characters are tied to the cemetery, but with so many prominent Wilmington figures buried on the grounds, it may not be surprising that some think the place is haunted.

Cotton Exchange

The Cotton Exchange isn't just the subject of one ghost story, but several. Tales claim that everything from Victorian-era ghosts to phantom soldiers occupy the space. There's also a pair of young ghosts that reportedly love to play mischievous pranks.

Burgwin-Wright House

Built in 1770 atop Wilmington's old jail, it's fitting that stories of colonial-era prisoners haunt the space. Some also claim to have seen a woman in white they believe to be a deceased member of the Wright family. Ghost stories at this historic downtown mansion have even managed to attract paranormal investigators in the past.

Poplar Grove Plantation

The Poplar Grove Plantation in Scotts Hill was owned by the Foy family for generations – and some of them allegedly remain as ghostly occupants of the home. Paranormal tours of the historic home are offered.

Charlie Kingree is the Pender County and trending topics reporter for the StarNews. He can be reached at ckingree@usatodayco.com.
